bw: Water, Na+ and K+ entering the nephron
tp: Almost 100 percent of glucose, amino acids and vitamins are also recovered in the PCT.

ww.About 10 percent: About 10 percent of water reaches the collecting ducts; most is recovered before then.
ww.About 99 percent: 99 percent is the total reabsorbed along the whole nephron.

evidence: About 67 percent of the water, Na+, and K+ entering the nephron is reabsorbed in the PCT and returned to the circulation.

tp: Basal Na+/K+ ATPase keeps Na+ low in the cell; the Na+ gradient then drives glucose in, and glucose leaves by facilitated diffusion.

ww.Simple diffusion: Glucose cannot cross unaided and moves against its gradient.
ww.Primary active transport: The glucose symporter itself uses the Na+ gradient, not ATP directly.

evidence: Glucose reabsorption in the kidneys is by secondary active transport.

tp: The transport maximum for glucose is about 375 mg/min in men and 300 mg/min in women.

ww.Proteinuria: Proteinuria is protein in the urine.
ww.Oliguria: Oliguria is too little urine output.

evidence: Though an exceptionally high sugar intake might cause sugar to appear briefly in the urine, the appearance of glycosuria usually points to type I or II diabetes mellitus.

bw: Water must follow Na+ pumped out of the PCT
tp: Water follows passively to keep the fluid in the peritubular capillary isotonic.

ww.Facultative water reabsorption: Facultative reabsorption is regulated by ADH in the collecting ducts rather than obliged by sodium.
ww.Countercurrent exchange: This describes opposing flows in the vasa recta and loop, not water following sodium.

evidence: This is called obligatory water reabsorption, because water is “obliged” to follow the Na+ (Figure 25.18).

bw: Enzyme in bicarbonate recovery by the PCT
Also used in red blood cells and the stomach
tp: Luminal HCO3- combines with H+ to form carbonic acid, which carbonic anhydrase converts to CO2 and water that enter the cell.

ww.Na+/K+ ATPase: This pump drives the sodium gradient but does not interconvert carbonic acid.
ww.Renin: Renin is the juxtaglomerular enzyme of the RAAS.

evidence: An important enzyme is used to catalyze this mechanism: carbonic anhydrase (CA).

bw: Part of the loop of Henle permeable to water
tp: Up to 15 percent of the water entering the nephron is reabsorbed here.

ww.Thick ascending limb: The ascending limb has no aquaporins and is impermeable to water.
ww.Distal convoluted tubule: The DCT is not part of the loop of Henle.

evidence: These membranes have permanent aquaporin channel proteins that allow unrestricted movement of water from the descending loop into the surrounding interstitium as osmolarity increases from about 300 mOsmol/kg to about 1200 mOsmol/kg.

bw: Loop of Henle section impermeable to water
tp: A Na+/K+/2Cl- symporter moves ions in, driven by the basal Na+/K+ ATPase; this also builds the hyperosmotic medulla.

ww.Descending loop: The descending loop is highly permeable to water.
ww.Collecting duct: Water permeability of the collecting duct depends on ADH.

evidence: As the loop turns to become the ascending loop, there is an absence of aquaporin channels, so water cannot leave the loop.

bw: Loop of Henle and vasa recta
tp: Solute pumps multiply the concentration of Na+ and urea deep in the medulla; the vasa recta must flow slowly to preserve it.

ww.Tubuloglomerular feedback: This is not described in the source as the loop’s concentrating mechanism.
ww.Renin-angiotensin system: The RAAS is a hormonal blood pressure and volume system.

evidence: The structure of the loop of Henle and associated vasa recta create a countercurrent multiplier system (Figure 25.20).

bw: Formed when amino acids are deaminated
tp: Urea is less toxic and helps the loop of Henle and collecting ducts recover water.

ww.Uric acid: The source does not describe uric acid as the deamination product converted to urea.

evidence: Ammonia (NH3) is a toxic byproduct of protein metabolism.

bw: Increases Na+/K+ ATPase in the basal membrane of the DCT and collecting duct
tp: Aldosterone also stimulates luminal Na+ and K+ channels in principal cells.

ww.ADH: ADH acts by inserting aquaporins and regulates water, not Na+ pumps.
ww.Parathyroid hormone: PTH induces calcium channels in the DCT.

evidence: Aldosterone increases the amount of Na+/K+ ATPase in the basal membrane of the DCT and collecting duct.

bw: Inserts calcium channels on the luminal surface
tp: Calcitriol also aids calcium recovery by inducing calcium-binding proteins.

ww.Calcitonin: The source does not describe calcitonin acting on the DCT.
ww.Aldosterone: Aldosterone regulates Na+ and K+ recovery.

evidence: Receptors for parathyroid hormone (PTH) are found in DCT cells and when bound to PTH, induce the insertion of calcium channels on their luminal surface.

bw: Inserts aquaporin channels into collecting duct principal cells
tp: Less ADH means fewer aquaporins, less water recovered and dilute urine.

ww.Angiotensin II: Angiotensin II is a vasoconstrictor that stimulates aldosterone and ADH release.

evidence: When stimulated by ADH, aquaporin channels are inserted into the apical membrane of principal cells, which line the collecting ducts.

bw: Collecting duct cells with channels for sodium and potassium
Have receptors for ADH and aldosterone
tp: Intercalated cells instead secrete or absorb acid or bicarbonate.

ww.Intercalated cells: Intercalated cells handle acid and bicarbonate.
ww.Podocytes: Podocytes are filtration cells of the glomerulus, not collecting duct cells.

evidence: A principal cell possesses channels for the recovery or loss of sodium and potassium.

bw: Secrete or absorb acid or bicarbonate
tp: They play significant roles in regulating blood pH.

ww.Principal cells: Principal cells handle Na+ and K+ and respond to ADH and aldosterone.

evidence: An intercalated cell secretes or absorbs acid or bicarbonate.

bw: Aldosterone raises Na+ recovery in the collecting duct
ans: More K+ is secreted into the urine
tp: When aldosterone falls, more Na+ stays in the urine and more K+ is retained.

ww.More K+ is reabsorbed: The Na+/K+ pump moves K+ in the opposite direction, into the forming urine.
ww.K+ is unchanged: K+ secretion rises in direct proportion to Na+ recovery.

evidence: As the pump recovers Na+ for the body, it is also pumping K+ into the forming urine, since the pump moves K+ in the opposite direction.

tp: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the rise and trigger ADH release from the posterior pituitary.

ww.Less water recovered, more urine: This is the response to falling plasma osmolarity.
ww.More Na+ lost, more urine: The response is regulated by ADH and conserves water.

evidence: If plasma osmolarity rises, more water is recovered and urine volume decreases; if plasma osmolarity decreases, less water is recovered and urine volume increases.
